note.note:
Consult Summary:
- Adult with prior childhood asthma presents with 2–3 days of wheeze and shortness of breath, likely asthma flare-up; plan includes increased inhaler use, addition of spacer and peak flow monitoring, and follow-up review.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Wheezing and sensation of shortness of breath for 2–3 days.
- Timeline: Symptoms began recently, lasting 2–3 days; similar episodes occurred in adulthood previously, but details unclear.
- Progression: Symptoms are ongoing; patient currently feels well at rest but reports recent limitation of activities (unable to walk to work, sometimes unable to complete sentences).
- Exacerbating factors: Not explicitly documented; possible triggers discussed include pollen or viral infection.
- Relieving factors: Not documented.
- Associated symptoms: Cough (without sputum or blood), subjective fever (patient reports temp measured at 37°C), no chest pain, no night-time waking, no chest pain, no phlegm production.
- Limitations: Unable to exercise or walk to work; sometimes finds it hard to finish sentences due to breathlessness.
- Current symptoms: No shortness of breath at rest, can go up and down stairs, currently feels well.
- Past symptom history: History of asthma as a child (severe; required medication and occasional hospital visits but no ICU), as well as hay fever and eczema. Last asthma medication used 3–4 years ago. Reports prior use of salbutamol "normally", especially with exercise (frequency: every few weeks). No recent routine inhaler medication except occasional salbutamol.
- Systems review: No chest pain, hemoptysis, or night-time symptoms; negative for other system involvement if not otherwise specified.

Past Medical History:
- Asthma in childhood (severe: required medication, hospital admissions, never ICU).
- Hay fever.
- Eczema.
- No other medical problems mentioned.
- Medications:
  - Salbutamol inhaler (dose/route/frequency not documented; used intermittently).
  - No medications for hay fever.
  - No other regular medications.
- Allergies: None reported.

Social History:
- Smoking: Non-smoker.
- Alcohol: Drinks one glass of wine every 2–3 days.
- Occupation: Engineer; used to walk to work but now working from home or on sick leave due to symptoms.
- Living circumstances: Lives with partner.

Family History:
- Not mentioned.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Patient self-reports temperature as 37°C.
- Other examination findings: Not documented.

Investigations:
- No laboratory or imaging studies performed or reported.
- Peak flow meter: To be prescribed for home monitoring.
- No other investigations noted.

Assessment & Plan:
- Issue 1: Asthma exacerbation (mild to moderate)
  - Likely asthma flare-up, possibly due to pollen or viral infection.
  - Advise increased use of salbutamol inhaler: 2–4 puffs every 4 hours (dose/frequency per conversation, actual prescribed dose not specified).
  - Prescribe spacer for inhaler delivery; pharmacist to provide teaching.
  - Prescribe peak flow meter for objective home monitoring.
  - Record peak flow readings morning and evening for one week; discuss results by telephone to assess control/change inhaler regimen if needed.
  - Arrange follow-up review in one week, or sooner if symptoms worsen (e.g., increased wheezing, high temperature).
- Issue 2: Hay fever
  - Recommend starting regular antihistamine (specific drug/dose/duration not specified; to be obtained from pharmacy).
- General plan:
  - Advise return/call if symptoms worsen acutely (e.g., high fever, increased wheeze, difficulty speaking).
  - Routine follow up and revisit medication regimen as needed.

Quality checks (always include at bottom of note, or fill document_quality):

●	Missing clinically expected elements: No complete medication reconciliation; doses/routes/frequency of inhaler therapy not fully documented; no detailed review of other systems; no documentation of family history; physical exam not performed (remote consult); no allergy to environmental agents discussed.
●	Internal conflicts: Unclear history regarding regularity of salbutamol use—patient notes both stopping inhalers 3–4 years ago and yet "normally" using salbutamol every few weeks (conflict noted).
●	Transcript quality: Clear, minimal background noise, some patient answers uncertain; key information captured but detail on some elements (medication names/family history) lacking.
